These vampires have trained themselves out of the traditional weaknesses, tolerating sunlight, garlic, and holy symbols, and they use the invitation to mesmerize the kingdom and take control. Granny Weatherwax, who feels her invitation was overlooked and is wrestling with doubts about her own worth, withdraws at first, leaving Nanny Ogg, Agnes Nitt, the returning Magrat, and a doubt-ridden young priest named Mightily Oats to resist. Agnes's divided mind gives her some protection against the vampires' influence, and Granny, once bitten, turns the connection to her advantage: her overwhelming will flows back down the blood-bond, saddling the Magpyrs with her own nature and cravings and stripping away their edge. Their much-vaunted self-training proves their undoing. With help from the coven, from Oats, who rediscovers his faith, and from the old traditional vampire the family had supplanted, the Magpyrs are destroyed. Lancre is freed, the royal baby is named in Granny's honour, and Granny recovers her sense of purpose.

recaps.text: Previously, in earlier books: the mountain kingdom of Lancre is guarded by a coven of witches led by the powerful and proud Granny Weatherwax and the warm, earthy Nanny Ogg. Over earlier adventures they saved Lancre's throne, traveled abroad where Granny defeated her own sister, and drove back the elves, after which the youngest of their old coven, Magrat Garlick, married King Verence II, the former royal Fool, and became queen. To fill the empty place in the coven, Granny and Nanny drew in Agnes Nitt, a young Lancre woman with a remarkable voice and, unusually, a second personality named Perdita sharing her head. Now Magrat and Verence have an infant daughter, and the kingdom has settled into a fragile peace. Granny remains its fiercest protector, but she is also its most troubled, prone to dark moods and, in this story, to gnawing doubts about whether her long life of hard choices has made her good or wicked.

King Verence of Lancre, anxious to be a modern and open-minded ruler, sends out invitations to the naming ceremony of his baby daughter, and among the guests he welcomes a family of vampires, the Magpyrs, who present themselves as civilized and enlightened. These vampires boast of having trained themselves out of the traditional weaknesses, so that sunlight, garlic, and holy symbols no longer trouble them. Granny Weatherwax's invitation appears to go astray, and, already burdened by doubts about her own worth, she takes the slight badly and holds herself apart. That leaves Nanny Ogg, Agnes Nitt, and the others to sense what the king in his tolerance cannot: that the polished, reasonable Magpyrs have not come to Lancre as guests at all, but as conquerors, and that the door has just been opened to let them in.

characters.description: A US Army Air Forces bombardier stationed on a Mediterranean island during the Second World War, consumed by the conviction that everyone, enemy and ally alike, is trying to kill him. Desperate to survive and to stop flying combat missions, he fakes illnesses to stay in the hospital and schemes for any way out, only to run up against the impossible regulation known as Catch-22.
characters.name: Yossarian

characters.description: The squadron's mess officer, a relentless entrepreneur who parlays his post into a sprawling black-market trading syndicate that he claims benefits everyone. Amoral and single-mindedly devoted to profit, he wheels and deals across the whole theater of war with cheerful disregard for its purpose.
characters.name: Milo Minderbinder

characters.description: The insecure, ambitious group commander desperate to be made a general and to see his name in the newspapers. To impress his superiors, he repeatedly raises the number of missions his men must fly, trapping airmen like Yossarian who are counting the days until they can go home.
characters.name: Colonel Cathcart

characters.description: The squadron's timid, well-meaning Anabaptist chaplain, lonely and unsure of his place amid the officers. Kindly and easily intimidated, he is troubled by the cruelty and absurdity around him and drawn to Yossarian's plight.
characters.name: Chaplain Tappman

characters.description: The self-pitying flight surgeon who bemoans his own bad luck at being sent to war. He is the one who first explains the logic of Catch-22 to Yossarian, showing why a man cannot be grounded for insanity if he is sane enough to ask to be grounded.
characters.name: Doc Daneeka

characters.description: A young, wealthy, earnest airman in Yossarian's outfit, decent and idealistic. He is hopelessly in love with a prostitute in Rome who is largely indifferent to him, and he dreams of a normal life after the war.
characters.name: Nately

characters.description: Yossarian's odd, tinkering tentmate, a small, grinning pilot who is forever repairing things and whose planes keep ditching in the sea. Cheerful and inscrutable, he seems always to be up to something no one else quite understands.
characters.name: Orr

characters.description: A hapless officer saddled with an absurd name and promoted to squadron commander by a clerical accident. Painfully awkward and desperate to avoid everyone, he will only see people in his office when he is known to be out of it.
characters.name: Major Major Major Major

characters.description: A jittery, wild-eyed airman tormented by screaming nightmares whenever he is not scheduled to fly a mission. Frantic and unstable, he obsessively tries to photograph women and embodies the fraying nerves of men pushed past their limits.
characters.name: Hungry Joe

characters.description: Colonel Cathcart's shrewd, cynical deputy, who does much of the real thinking behind the group's schemes. Sardonic and calculating, he manipulates his ambitious superior while looking after his own position.
characters.name: Colonel Korn

recaps.ending: Worn down by mounting deaths and the ever-rising mission count, and haunted above all by the memory of watching the young gunner Snowden die in his arms, Yossarian finally refuses to fly any more missions and walks around in protest. His commanders, Colonel Cathcart and Colonel Korn, embarrassed by his defiance, offer him a deal: they will send him home as a hero if he agrees to like them and to publicly endorse them, a bargain that would betray the other men still forced to fly. Yossarian nearly accepts, then rejects the corrupt offer. His decision is sealed when he learns that his odd tentmate Orr, whose repeated crash-landings turn out to have been deliberate practice, has made it safely to neutral Sweden. Seeing that escape is possible after all, Yossarian deserts, slipping away to strike out for Sweden himself and refusing any longer to be a pawn in a system that treats men's lives as expendable. His flight is an act of self-preservation and moral refusal, choosing his own survival and conscience over an insane war and the ambitions of the men running it.
recaps.in_short: During the Second World War, bombardier Yossarian is stationed with an American bomber group on a Mediterranean island, certain that everyone is trying to kill him and desperate to be grounded before he is killed. He is thwarted by Catch-22, the maddening rule that a man must be crazy to keep flying missions but that anyone who asks to be excused thereby proves he is sane and must keep flying. His scheming commander, Colonel Cathcart, keeps raising the number of missions required, so the finish line is never reached. Around Yossarian swirls a cast of absurd figures, including the profiteering mess officer Milo Minderbinder, whose black-market syndicate consumes the war effort, and the meek chaplain. As friends die one after another and the horror of a gunner's death aboard his plane finally overwhelms him, Yossarian resolves to stop cooperating. Offered a corrupt bargain to go home in exchange for praising his superiors, he refuses, and, learning that the vanished Orr has escaped to neutral Sweden, he deserts to try to follow him.

recaps.text: The novel is set during the Second World War on the small Mediterranean island of Pianosa, where an American bombing group flies missions over Italy. Its central figure is Yossarian, a bombardier gripped by the certainty that everyone, the enemy above and his own commanders below, is out to kill him, and obsessed with staying alive. He takes refuge in the base hospital by faking ailments, anything to avoid flying more combat missions. His great obstacle is Catch-22, the circular regulation holding that a flier must be insane to be excused from missions, yet any man who requests to be excused proves by his concern for his own safety that he is sane, and so must keep flying. Around Yossarian moves a large cast of officers and airmen rendered by turns comic and horrifying, and his commander keeps raising the number of missions required, ensuring the ordeal never ends. Told out of order and in a darkly absurd key, the story circles the madness and cruelty of the war.
